top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B040) is a mature conceptual advance with the cleanest attribution on the slate. The 1997 collateral-constraint mechanism links credit limits to asset prices, so small shocks become large and persistent. It has had nearly three decades of extension, criticism and use in macro-finance and policy models. The originating contribution sits with two people, so a two-name part leaves no co-originator out. The citation should claim the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles are modelled, not a settled amplification magnitude. The main costs are indirect empirical validation, the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist, and some residual overlap with the 2022 prize. I find the mechanism distinction credible, though I have not verified it against the 2022 background. I rank P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, anchored on trade-shock evidence) second. Its attribution is clean and its identification is direct, but the record is about a decade old and shift-share inference and effect sizes are still debated. P003 is a substantive but mainly methodological contribution, and its functional-form sensitivity and boundary cuts weigh against it. I still rank it above no award because it is a real, mature achievement.
recusal_note: No tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn is apparent from the profile. I co-author with chair John Hassler (who supports P001) and secretary Per Krusell (who supports P002), and I am their IIES colleague. My research is in macroeconomics, the same broad field as P001. My long-running collaborators Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li are not credited on any proposal on the slate. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated.
